title: Prefixes
blurb: Read the prefixes the TEAS tests (number, place, time, negation and amount) and never fall for hypo/hyper, inter/intra or ante/anti.
question: A chart note says one patient needs an intramuscular injection and another has intercostal pain. A third has hypoglycemia, not hyperglycemia. How do the prefixes alone tell you where each problem is and which way each value has moved?

teach.body: Formally, a prefix is a word part attached to the front of a root that modifies its meaning, usually telling where, when, how much or whether not. In plain English: the root says what the word is about, and the prefix says which way to turn it. Hyper- and hypo- attach to the same root but point in opposite directions, so one misread prefix flips the whole answer.

Meaning
Example

teach.caption: Also: auto- (self), co-, con-, syn- (with, together), de- (down, remove), dis- (apart, not), ultra- (beyond).

teach.h: inter- vs intra-, ante- vs anti-
teach.caption: Interstate highways run BETWEEN states; an intranet stays WITHIN one company.
Prefix modifies, root gives the core meaning, suffix gives the part of speech.

teach.body: Diego Ramirez, a CNA applying to an LPN program, reads a care plan: 'subcutaneous injection, monitor for tachycardia, bilateral leg swelling, postoperative day 2.' He works prefix by prefix. Sub- = under, so the injection goes under the skin. Tachy- = fast, so he watches for a fast heart rate. Bi- = two, so both legs are swollen. Post- = after, so it is the second day after surgery. No medical training needed: just the parts.

teach.text: Look-alikes the TEAS uses as distractors: hyper/hypo, inter/intra, ante/anti, pre/post, dys/dis (dys- = bad or difficult; dis- = apart or not), peri/para (around vs beside). And in- has two meanings: 'not' (inactive) but also 'into' (inhale). 'Inflammable' means flammable, not fireproof.

items: A prefix sits in front of the root and modifies it: where, when, how much or not.
Number: mono/uni 1, bi/di 2, tri 3, quadri/tetra 4, hemi/semi half, poly/multi many, pan all.
Place: sub under, supra above, epi upon, peri around, inter between, intra within, trans across.
Opposites: hypo/hyper, brady/tachy, pre/post, ab/ad, dys/eu, endo/exo.
Never read the root alone: hypoglycemia is LOW blood sugar.

summary: You can now read the prefixes the TEAS tests for number, position, time, negation and amount, and use them to pin down a word's meaning. You can also separate the classic look-alikes: hypo/hyper, inter/intra, ante/anti, dys/dis and peri/para.

A.q: Based on its word parts, what does "hypoglycemia" mean?
A.why: Hypo- means below or deficient, glyc means sugar and -emia means a blood condition: a low level of sugar in the blood.

whyNot.1: High blood sugar is hyperglycemia; hyper- means above or excessive.
whyNot.2: -emia refers to blood, not urine (a urine condition uses -uria).
whyNot.3: glyc means sugar, not fat (fat is lip/o), and hypo- means low, not high.

A.q: In the word "intramuscular," the prefix intra- means
A.why: Intra- means within, so an intramuscular injection is given within a muscle.

whyNot.0: Between is inter-, the classic look-alike (intercostal = between the ribs).
whyNot.2: Across is trans- (transdermal = across the skin).
whyNot.3: Beneath is sub- (subcutaneous = beneath the skin).

A.q: Which word contains a prefix meaning "against"?
A.why: Anti- means against: an antibiotic acts against living bacteria.

whyNot.0: Ante- means before; antenatal means before birth. It looks like anti- but means something different.
whyNot.2: Pro- in prognosis means before (a forecast of the course of a disease).
whyNot.3: Post- means after: postoperative means after surgery.

B.q: A patient with bradycardia has a heart rate that is
B.why: Brady- means slow and cardi means heart, so bradycardia is a slow heart rate.

whyNot.1: A fast heart rate is tachycardia; tachy- means fast.
whyNot.2: Brady- refers to speed, not regularity of rhythm.
whyNot.3: Heart pain would use a pain suffix such as -algia or -dynia; brady- means slow.

B.q: Which prefix, added to "-cardium," names the sac that lies AROUND the heart?
B.why: Peri- means around, so the pericardium is the sac around the heart.

whyNot.0: Epi- means upon or over: the epicardium lies on the heart's surface.
whyNot.1: Endo- means within: the endocardium lines the inside of the heart.
whyNot.3: Para- means beside, beyond or abnormal, not around; it is the classic peri- look-alike.

B.q: A warning label describes a cleaning spray as "inflammable." What does the label mean?
options: The spray will not catch fire
The spray is safe near flames
The spray puts out small fires
B.why: In "inflammable," in- does not mean "not": inflammable means the same as flammable, so the spray catches fire easily.

whyNot.0: This reads in- as "not," the trap the TEAS sets: inflammable means flammable.
whyNot.2: This also misreads in- as "not"; an inflammable spray is dangerous near flames.
whyNot.3: Nothing in the word means putting out fire; it describes material that burns.

C.q: Which pair of words contains prefixes with OPPOSITE meanings?
C.why: Sub- means under or below and supra- means above or over, so their meanings are opposites.

whyNot.0: Intra- and endo- both mean within: they are synonyms, not opposites.
whyNot.1: Circum- and peri- both mean around.
whyNot.2: Bi- and du- both mean two.

C.q: A pharmacist says a medicine is "contraindicated" for a patient. Based on the prefix, what should happen with that medicine?
options: Give it at a lower dose
C.why: Contra- means against: a contraindication is a reason against using something, so the medicine should be avoided for that patient.

whyNot.0: This confuses contra- (against) with co- or con- (with, together).
whyNot.1: A lower amount would point to a prefix such as hypo- (deficient); contra- means against.
whyNot.3: Before would be pre- or ante-; contra- means against.

C.q: Based on its prefix, "retroperitoneal" describes a structure located
C.why: Retro- means backward or behind, so retroperitoneal means behind the peritoneum.

whyNot.0: Within would be intra- or endo-.
whyNot.1: Around would be peri- or circum-.

reteach.title: Prefixes are like little direction words
reteach.question: Think of the words you use to give directions: under, over, around, across. How do prefixes do the same job for a root?

blocks.h: Root = the place, prefix = where you are
blocks.body: Picture a bridge. You can be under it, over it, around it, across it or behind it. The bridge never changes, but your position does. A root works the same way: the skin (cutane) stays the skin, while sub- puts you under it, epi- upon it and trans- across it. Learn the direction words once and they work on every root you meet.

blocks.text: Between two things (inter-) is not the same as inside one thing (intra-). Interstate travel crosses state lines; intrastate travel stays inside one state.

explain.body: mono-/uni- one, bi-/di-/du- two, tri- three, quadri-/tetra- four, hemi-/semi- half, multi-/poly- many, pan- all.

test.q: Based on its prefix, "polyuria" describes urine that is
test.why: Poly- means many or much and -uria means a urine condition: urine produced in excessive amounts.

whyNot.1: Pain or difficulty would be signaled by dys-, not poly-.
whyNot.2: Poly- means many or much, the opposite of small amounts.
whyNot.3: Blood in the urine is hematuria (hemat = blood); poly- says nothing about blood.

explain.body: sub- under, supra-/super- above, epi- upon, peri-/circum- around, inter- between, intra-/endo- within, ex-/exo- out, trans- across, retro- behind.

test.q: Which word describes something located between the ribs?
test.why: Inter- means between and cost means rib: intercostal means between the ribs.

whyNot.0: Intra- means within, not between: the classic inter/intra mix-up.
whyNot.1: Sub- means below, so subcostal means below the ribs.
whyNot.3: Supra- means above, so supracostal means above the ribs.

explain.body: a-/an-/non-/in- not or without, anti-/contra- against, dys- bad or difficult, eu- good or normal, mal- bad, mis- wrongly. Do not confuse dys- with dis- (apart, not).

test.q: Based on its word parts, "dysphagia" means
options: loss of the ability to speak
test.why: Dys- means bad, difficult or painful and -phagia means eating or swallowing: difficult swallowing.

whyNot.0: Normal function would use eu-, the opposite of dys-.
whyNot.1: Speech is -phasia (aphasia); -phagia refers to swallowing. The two suffixes look alike.
whyNot.2: Excess would be signaled by hyper- or poly-; dys- means difficult.

explain.body: ante-/pre-/pro- before, post- after, neo- new, re- again. brady- slow, tachy- fast. ante- (before) looks like anti- (against).

test.q: Which word refers to the period BEFORE birth?
test.why: Ante- means before, so antenatal means before birth.

whyNot.0: Post- means after: postnatal is after birth.
whyNot.1: Neo- means new: neonatal refers to the newborn.
whyNot.3: Anti- means against, not before; this is the ante/anti trap.
